question:
A 38-year-old woman is evaluated for a difficult-to-control hypertension. Her symptoms include sleep interruption because of frequent waking up for voiding and frequent headaches. She has smoked 10 cigarettes daily for the past 5 years. Family history is insignificant. Her vital signs include a blood pressure of 170/96 mm Hg, pulse of 90/min, and temperature of 36.7°C (98.0°F). Physical examination is unremarkable. Her lab results are shown:
Serum sodium 146 mEq/L
Serum potassium 4 mEq/L
Serum bicarbonate 29 mEq/L
Her plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC): plasma renin activity (PRA) ratio measured after following all precautions is found to be elevated. Oral salt loading testing reveals a lack of aldosterone suppression. A computerized tomography (CT) scan of the adrenal glands shows a 2 cm mass on the left side. Which of the following is the best next step for this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Elevated PAC:PRA ratio -> suspicion of primary hyperaldosteronism -> 80% CHAIN: Lack of aldosterone suppression on salt loading test -> confirms primary hyperaldosteronism -> 85% CHAIN: 2 cm mass on the left adrenal gland -> suggestive of an aldosterone-producing adenoma -> 90% CHAIN: Best next step for this patient -> Adrenal venous sampling to confirm the source of aldosterone excess -> 80%
enhanced_information: The patient likely has primary hyperaldosteronism due to an aldosterone-producing adenoma based on an elevated PAC:PRA ratio, lack of aldosterone suppression on salt loading test, and presence of a 2 cm mass on the left adrenal gland. The best next step is adrenal venous sampling to confirm the source of aldosterone excess, which aligns with standard practice. Evidence paths mentioning Conn Syndrome and Conn Adenoma support the suspicion of an adenoma in this case.
analysis: The patient likely has primary hyperaldosteronism due to an aldosterone-producing adenoma, supported by an elevated PAC:PRA ratio, lack of aldosterone suppression on salt loading test, and the presence of a 2 cm mass on the left adrenal gland. Adrenal venous sampling is the best next step to confirm the source of aldosterone excess and guide further management.
